content: The market landscape in 2026 is characterized by strong expectations of continued revenue improvements and overarching economic resilience [1] [2] [3] . The ongoing contributions of new, state-of-the-art property developments continue to shape the industrial landscape, reinforcing the sector's capacity to meet the complex, evolving operational requirements of modern industrial, manufacturing, and mining enterprises [5] . Academic research contextualizes these conflicts within a broader neoliberal framework, highlighting the structural tensions between corporate profit priorities and the fundamental rights of affected rural populations, particularly concerning environmental justice and corporate accountability [55] . Holding mining land as a property asset requires a comprehensive understanding of the overlapping liabilities that can significantly degrade land value and impose severe financial burdens on property owners and operators. Consequently, the legal obligations tied to mining land are perpetual and require continuous financial provisioning. Efforts to combat environmental liabilities are further enforced by the "polluter pays" principle, legally requiring mining companies to allocate substantial funds for the remediation of any environmental damage caused by their operations [74] . However, the practical application and enforcement of these frameworks remain inadequate to handle the sheer scale of the historical and ongoing environmental crises [56] . Resolving these overlapping liabilities requires robust policies, stringent enforcement mechanisms, and significant financial and technical interventions [64] [75] .
